claim: Aberrant activation of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) has been described in a range of human cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer and neuroblastoma.
source: Aberrant activation of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) has been described in a range of human cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer and neuroblastoma (Hallberg and Palmer, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hallberg and Palmer, 2013.

claim: Vertebrate ALK has been considered to be an orphan receptor.
source: Vertebrate ALK has been considered to be an orphan receptor and the identity of the ALK ligand(s) is a critical issue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are potent ligands for human ALK.
source: Here we show that FAM150A and FAM150B are potent ligands for human ALK that bind to the extracellular domain of ALK and in addition to activation of wild-type ALK are able to drive 'superactivation' of activated ALK mutants from neuroblastoma.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments shown in the figures.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B bind to the extracellular domain of ALK.
source: Here we show that FAM150A and FAM150B are potent ligands for human ALK that bind to the extracellular domain of ALK and in addition to activation of wild-type ALK are able to drive 'superactivation' of activated ALK mutants from neuroblastoma.
evidence: This is supported by binding assays shown in Figure 4A and immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are able to drive 'superactivation' of activated ALK mutants from neuroblastoma.
source: Here we show that FAM150A and FAM150B are potent ligands for human ALK that bind to the extracellular domain of ALK and in addition to activation of wild-type ALK are able to drive 'superactivation' of activated ALK mutants from neuroblastoma.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F-G demonstrating increased activation of ALK mutants by FAM150A/B.

claim: ALK activation is commonly due to fusion of the ALK kinase domain with a dimerization partner that drives activation.
source: Activation of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is commonly due to fusion of the ALK kinase domain with a dimerization partner that drives activation, however, ALK activation also occurs in the context of the full length receptor, for example, as activating point mutations in neuroblastoma (Maris et al., 2007; Carén et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2008; George et al., 2008; Janoueix-Lerosey et al., 2008; Mosseé et al., 2008; Hallberg and Palmer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ALK activation occurs in the context of the full length receptor as activating point mutations in neuroblastoma.
source: Activation of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is commonly due to fusion of the ALK kinase domain with a dimerization partner that drives activation, however, ALK activation also occurs in the context of the full length receptor, for example, as activating point mutations in neuroblastoma (Maris et al., 2007; Carén et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2008; George et al., 2008; Janoueix-Lerosey et al., 2008; Mosseé et al., 2008; Hallberg and Palmer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In many tumor types ALK overexpression and activation has been described.
source: In many additional tumor types ALK overexpression and activation has been described, and it is unclear whether this is dependent on the activity of a ligand (Hallberg and Palmer 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hallberg and Palmer 2013.

claim: It is unclear whether ALK overexpression and activation in many tumor types is dependent on the activity of a ligand.
source: In many additional tumor types ALK overexpression and activation has been described, and it is unclear whether this is dependent on the activity of a ligand (Hallberg and Palmer 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field, with citation to prior work.

claim: The ALK receptor in Drosophila has a well defined ligand called Jeb.
source: The ALK receptors in both Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans  have well defined ligands – Jeb (Englund et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2003; Stute et al., 2004) and HEN-1 (Ishihara et al., 2002), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ALK receptor in Caenorhabditis elegans has a well defined ligand called HEN-1.
source: The ALK receptors in both Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans  have well defined ligands – Jeb (Englund et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2003; Stute et al., 2004) and HEN-1 (Ishihara et al., 2002), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Vertebrate ALK has long been considered as an orphan receptor.
source: In contrast, vertebrate ALK has long been considered as an orphan receptor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The human ALK locus encodes a classical receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) comprising a unique extracellular ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane domain and an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain.
source: The human ALK locus encodes a classical receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) comprising a unique extracellular ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane domain and an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain (Hallberg and Palmer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The extracellular portion of ALK contains two MAM domains, a glycine-rich region (GR) and a LDLa domain.
source: The extracellular portion of ALK which contains two MAM domains (named after meprin, A-5 protein and receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase μ), a glycine-rich region (GR) and a LDLa domain, is unique among the RTKs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ALK structure.

claim: The extracellular portion of ALK is unique among the RTKs.
source: The extracellular portion of ALK which contains two MAM domains (named after meprin, A-5 protein and receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase μ), a glycine-rich region (GR) and a LDLa domain, is unique among the RTKs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ALK structure.

claim: ALK and the related leukocyte tyrosine kinase (LTK) RTK share kinase domain similarities.
source: ALK, and the related leukocyte tyrosine kinase (LTK) RTK, share kinase domain similarities as well as a GR in the membrane proximal portion of their extracellular domains (ECDs) (Iwahara et al., 1997; Morris et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ALK and LTK share a glycine-rich region (GR) in the membrane proximal portion of their extracellular domains.
source: ALK, and the related leukocyte tyrosine kinase (LTK) RTK, share kinase domain similarities as well as a GR in the membrane proximal portion of their extracellular domains (ECDs) (Iwahara et al., 1997; Morris et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B were identified as ligands for LTK through screening of the extracellular proteome.
source: Recent screening of the extracellular proteome identified two novel secreted proteins as ligands for LTK – family with sequence similarity 150A (FAM150A) and family with sequence similarity 150B (FAM150B). Both bind to the ECD of the receptor leading to activation of downstream signaling in cell culture models (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B bind to the ECD of LTK leading to activation of downstream signaling in cell culture models.
source: Recent screening of the extracellular proteome identified two novel secreted proteins as ligands for LTK – family with sequence similarity 150A (FAM150A) and family with sequence similarity 150B (FAM150B). Both bind to the ECD of the receptor leading to activation of downstream signaling in cell culture models (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are unique, displaying homology only with one another but not with any other proteins in mammals.
source: FAM150A and FAM150B are unique, displaying homology only with one another but not with any other proteins in mammals (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: FAM150B is strongly expressed in the human adrenal gland.
source: Furthermore, we found the reported strong expression of FAM150B in the human adrenal gland (Zhang et al., 2014) intriguing, given the role of ALK in neuroblastoma.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B activate ALK signaling in PC12 cell neurite outgrowth assays.
source: We investigated ALK activation by FAM150A and FAM150B proteins in PC12 cell neurite outgrowth assays where we observed a strong activation of ALK signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Conditioned medium containing either FAM150A or FAM150B was able to activate endogenous ALK signaling in neuroblastoma cells.
source: Conditioned medium containing either FAM150A or FAM150B was able to activate endogenous ALK signaling in neuroblastoma cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are able to robustly drive human ALK activation when ectopically coexpressed in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: We also employed the model organism Drosophila melanogaster as a readout for activation of ALK by FAM150A and FAM150B, showing that FAM150 proteins are able to robustly drive human ALK activation when ectopically coexpressed in the fly.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The GR of the ALK receptor ECD is important for FAM150 activation.
source: The GR of the ALK receptor ECD is important for FAM150 activation, and monoclonal antibodies (mAb) recognizing the GR of ALK are able to inhibit activation of ALK by FAM150A.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4E.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies recognizing the GR of ALK are able to inhibit activation of ALK by FAM150A.
source: The GR of the ALK receptor ECD is important for FAM150 activation, and monoclonal antibodies (mAb) recognizing the GR of ALK are able to inhibit activation of ALK by FAM150A.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ALK and LTK share similarity in their membrane proximal ECD in the form of a glycine-rich domain that is approximately 250 amino acids in length.
source: ALK and the related LTK share similarity in their membrane proximal ECD in the form of a glycine-rich domain that is ∼250 amino acids in length (Figure 1A, GR depicted in grey).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The glycine-rich domain of ALK and LTK contains multiple runs of up to eight glycine residues.
source: This domain contains multiple runs of up to eight glycine residues, and is unique to ALK and LTK within the human genome.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of the domain.

claim: The glycine-rich domain is unique to ALK and LTK within the human genome.
source: This domain contains multiple runs of up to eight glycine residues, and is unique to ALK and LTK within the human genome.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of the domain.

claim: Four independent point mutations in the glycine-rich region leading to exchange of single glycine residues result in complete loss of function of Drosophila ALK in vivo.
source: The importance of the GR in ALK has been highlighted in Drosophila studies, where four independent point mutations leading to exchange of single glycine residues result in complete loss of function in vivo (Englund et al., 2003) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Englund et al., 2003 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The similarity between ALK and LTK within the GR is approximately 70%, with amino acid identity of 55%.
source: The similarity between ALK and LTK within the GR is ∼70%, with amino acid identity of 55%, containing a total of 51 conserved glycine residues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the alignment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The GR of ALK and LTK contains a total of 51 conserved glycine residues.
source: The similarity between ALK and LTK within the GR is ∼70%, with amino acid identity of 55%, containing a total of 51 conserved glycine residues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the alignment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of either FAM150A or FAM150B alone in PC12 cells did not lead to neurite outgrowth activation.
source: Expression of either FAM150A, or FAM150B or ALK alone, did not lead to activation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Expression of ALK alone in PC12 cells did not lead to neurite outgrowth activation.
source: Expression of either FAM150A, or FAM150B or ALK alone, did not lead to activation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: ALK-F1174L is a constitutively active ALK neuroblastoma mutation.
source: This was in contrast to the strong activation seen with the positive control ALK-F1174L which is a well characterized constitutively active ALK neuroblastoma mutation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about this mutation.

claim: Coexpression of FAM150A with ALK led to robust activation of ALK neurite outgrowth activity in PC12 cells.
source: However, coexpression with either FAM150A or FAM150B led to robust activation of ALK neurite outgrowth activity (Figure 1C, quantified in 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Coexpression of FAM150B with ALK led to robust activation of ALK neurite outgrowth activity in PC12 cells.
source: However, coexpression with either FAM150A or FAM150B led to robust activation of ALK neurite outgrowth activity (Figure 1C, quantified in 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: ALK activation by FAM150A and FAM150B was visualized by phosphorylation of Y1604 in the tail of the ALK intracellular domain.
source: This ALK activation was visualized by phosphorylation of Y1604 in the tail of the ALK intracellular domain (Figure 1E, F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and was further associated with stimulation of downstream signaling such as the phosphorylation of the downstream target ERK1/2 (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: ALK activation by FAM150A and FAM150B was associated with stimulation of downstream signaling such as the phosphorylation of ERK1/2.
source: This ALK activation was visualized by phosphorylation of Y1604 in the tail of the ALK intracellular domain (Figure 1E, F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and was further associated with stimulation of downstream signaling such as the phosphorylation of the downstream target ERK1/2 (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Addition of conditioned medium from cells expressing FAM150A or FAM150B led to strong activation of ALK in PC12 cells expressing ALK.
source: Addition of conditioned medium from cells expressing FAM150A or FAM150B led to strong activation of ALK in receiving cells that expressed ALK, as measured by neurite outgrowth and activation of downstream signaling (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: ALK signaling activity induced by either FAM150A or FAM150B was inhibited by addition of 250 nM crizotinib.
source: We observed that ALK activation by FAM150A or FAM150B was inhibited by addition of 250 nM crizotinib (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Exogenously produced FAM150A and FAM150B proteins stimulate ALK signaling in IMR-32 cells.
source: Thus we observed that exogenously produced FAM150A and FAM150B proteins stimulate ALK signaling in both PC12 cells and IMR-32 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Robust activation of ALK by FAM150A-containing or FAM150B-containing conditioned medium was observed in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells.
source: To address whether endogenous levels of ALK responded to medium conditioned with either FAM150A or FAM150B, we employed the IMR-32 neuroblastoma cell line that expresses wild-type ALK. Once again, we observed robust activation of ALK by the addition of either FAM150A-containing or FAM150B-containing conditioned medium, employing pALK-Y1604 and pERK1/2 as readout (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The activation of ALK and downstream signaling events in IMR-32 cells were effectively blocked by the addition of 250 nM crizotinib.
source: The activation of ALK and downstream signaling events in IMR-32 cells were effectively blocked by the addition of 250 nM crizotinib (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Recombinant FAM150A purified from Sf21 cells activates exogenous ALK in PC12 cells and endogenous ALK in IMR-32 cells.
source: The activation of exogenous ALK in PC12 cells or endogenous ALK in IMR-32 cells was reproduced with the addition of recombinant FAM150A purified from Sf21 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ALK activation by FAM150A or FAM150B containing conditioned media in IMR-32 cells was observed at 2–5 min, peaking around 20 min before decreasing at later time points.
source: More careful examination of ALK activation by FAM150A or FAM150B containing conditioned media in IMR-32 cells revealed activation of signaling at 2–5 min, peaking around 20 min before decreasing at later time points.
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: ALK activation by FAM150A/B was observed at the level of ALK receptor phosphorylation (pALK-Y1604), and with downstream pERK5 and pERK1/2.
source: This response was observed at the level of ALK receptor phosphorylation (pALK-Y1604), and with downstream pERK5 (Umapathy et al., 2014) and pERK1/2 (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: No additional activation of ALK by FAM150 proteins was observed in the presence of heparin.
source: While we were able to see strong binding of purified FAM150A protein as well as FAM150A-HA and FAM150B-HA from conditioned medium to heparin-agarose, we did not observe any additional activation of ALK by FAM150 proteins in the presence of heparin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither the Drosophila Alk ligand Jeb nor previously proposed vertebrate ligands (human midkine and pleiotrophin) are able to activate either mouse or human ALK.
source: Neither the Drosophila Alk ligand Jeb (Englund et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2003; Stute et al., 2004) nor previously proposed vertebrate ligands, that is, human midkine (MDK) and pleiotrophin (PTN) are able to activate either mouse or human ALK (Yang et al., 2007; Hugosson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Expression of either FAM150A or FAM150B in the developing Drosophila eye using the GMR-Gal4 driver resulted in normal eye morphology.
source: Expression of either FAM150A or FAM150B in the developing eye, using the GMR-Gal4 driver, resulted in normal eye morphology (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of constitutively active ALK-F1174S in the Drosophila eye results in a rough eye morphology.
source: In contrast, expression of constitutively active ALK-F1174S described in neuroblastoma patients results in a rough eye morphology (Figure 3A) (Martinsson et al., 2011), while no eye phenotype was observed upon the expression of wild-type human ALK alone (Figure 3A) (Martinsson et al., 2011, Schonherr, Ruuth et al., 2011, Schonherr, Ruuth et al., 2011, Chand et al., 2013; Hugosson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior literature.

claim: No eye phenotype was observed upon the expression of wild-type human ALK alone in Drosophila.
source: In contrast, expression of constitutively active ALK-F1174S described in neuroblastoma patients results in a rough eye morphology (Figure 3A) (Martinsson et al., 2011), while no eye phenotype was observed upon the expression of wild-type human ALK alone (Figure 3A) (Martinsson et al., 2011, Schonherr, Ruuth et al., 2011, Schonherr, Ruuth et al., 2011, Chand et al., 2013; Hugosson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior literature.

claim: Coexpression of either FAM150A or FAM150B together with human ALK in the Drosophila eye led to a rough eye phenotype.
source: This can be compared with coexpression of either FAM150A or FAM150B together with human ALK which led to a rough eye phenotype, proving that both FAM150A and FAM150B were able to activate human ALK in this in vivo system (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Both FAM150A and FAM150B are able to activate human ALK in the Drosophila in vivo system.
source: This can be compared with coexpression of either FAM150A or FAM150B together with human ALK which led to a rough eye phenotype, proving that both FAM150A and FAM150B were able to activate human ALK in this in vivo system (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Purified human FAM150A binds to ALK-ECD-Fc with a dissociation constant of approximately 20 nM.
source: Purified human FAM150A (Zhang et al., 2014) binds to ALK-ECD-Fc with a dissociation constant of ∼20 nM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Biacore SPR analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both FAM150A and FAM150B can be independently immunoprecipitated with the ALK receptor.
source: Here we observed that both FAM150A and FAM150B could be independently immunoprecipitated with the ALK receptor, and that ALK could be immunoprecipitated with either FAM150A or FAM150B in the reciprocal pull-down experiments (Figure 4B, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: ALK can be immunoprecipitated with either FAM150A or FAM150B in reciprocal pull-down experiments.
source: Here we observed that both FAM150A and FAM150B could be independently immunoprecipitated with the ALK receptor, and that ALK could be immunoprecipitated with either FAM150A or FAM150B in the reciprocal pull-down experiments (Figure 4B, C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Both ALK and FAM150A immunoprecipitate with LTK.
source: Since FAM150A/B also bind LTK, we asked whether ALK and LTK interacted in the presence of FAM150A. Indeed, both ALK and FAM150A were found to immunoprecipitate with LTK (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Binding of FAM150A and FAM150B to ALK on the cell surface leads to uptake and internalization of the ALK-FAM150 complex.
source: In these experiments we observed uptake of FAM150A and FAM150B into ALK-positive intracellular vesicles, suggesting that binding to ALK on the cell surface leads to uptake and internalization of the ALK-FAM150 complex (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from immunofluorescence data showing intracellular vesicles positive for both ALK and FAM150A/B in Figure 4D.

claim: Deletion of the GR in the ALK ECD did not affect FAM150A binding.
source: Deletion of the GR in the ALK ECD did not affect FAM150A binding but led to loss of FAM150B binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Deletion of the GR in the ALK ECD led to loss of FAM150B binding.
source: Deletion of the GR in the ALK ECD did not affect FAM150A binding but led to loss of FAM150B binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: All four glycine mutations (G740D, G823D, G893E and G934D) in the GR severely impaired binding of FAM150B to ALK.
source: Despite being well expressed, all four glycine mutations in the GR severely impaired binding of FAM150B to ALK.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Mutation of individual glycines in the GR had no effect on the FAM150A-ALK interaction.
source: Consistent with our earlier results we were unable to see any effect of mutation of individual glycine on the FAM150A-ALK interaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: mAb13 exhibited strong inhibition of FAM150A-induced ALK activation.
source: While mAb135 had no effect on FAM150A activation of ALK, we observed that mAb13 exhibited strong inhibition of FAM150A-induced ALK activation (Figure 4E), while mAb48 robustly activated ALK in the absence of FAM150A ligand (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: mAb48 robustly activated ALK in the absence of FAM150A ligand.
source: While mAb135 had no effect on FAM150A activation of ALK, we observed that mAb13 exhibited strong inhibition of FAM150A-induced ALK activation (Figure 4E), while mAb48 robustly activated ALK in the absence of FAM150A ligand (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: mAb135 had no effect on FAM150A activation of ALK.
source: While mAb135 had no effect on FAM150A activation of ALK, we observed that mAb13 exhibited strong inhibition of FAM150A-induced ALK activation (Figure 4E), while mAb48 robustly activated ALK in the absence of FAM150A ligand (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B activate the ALK-R1275Q mutant to a higher level in PC12 cells.
source: In PC12 cells we indeed observed activation of the ALK-R1275Q mutant to a higher level, as evidenced by increased pERK1/2 and in neurite outgrowth assays (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B increase activation of ERK1/2 in CLB-GAR cells which endogenously express the ALK-R1275Q mutant.
source: This increased activity was also seen in CLB-GAR cells, which endogenously express the ALK-R1275Q mutant, with increased activation of ERK1/2 upon the addition of either FAM150A or FAM150B (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A similar superactivation effect was observed with the ALK-F1174L mutant.
source: A similar effect was observed with the ALK-F1174L mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: A number of independent studies have presented convincing evidence that MDK and PTN do not activate ALK.
source: However, a number of independent studies including our own work have presented convincing evidence that MDK and PTN do not activate ALK (Motegi et al., 2004; Moog-Lutz et al., 2005; Mourali et al., 2006; Mathivet et al., 2007; Hugosson et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Long chain heparins have been identified as activators of ALK in neuroblastoma cells.
source: The recent identification of long chain heparins as activators of ALK in neuroblastoma cells (Murray et al., 2015) and the interplay of this with ALK activation by FAM150A and FAM150B will require further work.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2015.

claim: FAM150A has a predicted pI of 10.6.
source: FAM150A and FAM150B are very basic proteins; FAM150A has a predicted pI of 10.6, while FAM150B has one of 9.75, and we show here that FAM150A exhibits heparin binding properties, however we have not observed a cooperative role of heparin and the FAM150 ligands in ALK activation as has been described for the fibroblast growth factor receptors and FGF.
evidence: This is stated as a calculated property of the protein.

claim: FAM150B has a predicted pI of 9.75.
source: FAM150A and FAM150B are very basic proteins; FAM150A has a predicted pI of 10.6, while FAM150B has one of 9.75, and we show here that FAM150A exhibits heparin binding properties, however we have not observed a cooperative role of heparin and the FAM150 ligands in ALK activation as has been described for the fibroblast growth factor receptors and FGF.
evidence: This is stated as a calculated property of the protein.

claim: FAM150A exhibits heparin binding properties.
source: FAM150A and FAM150B are very basic proteins; FAM150A has a predicted pI of 10.6, while FAM150B has one of 9.75, and we show here that FAM150A exhibits heparin binding properties, however we have not observed a cooperative role of heparin and the FAM150 ligands in ALK activation as has been described for the fibroblast growth factor receptors and FGF.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No cooperative role of heparin and the FAM150 ligands in ALK activation was observed.
source: FAM150A and FAM150B are very basic proteins; FAM150A has a predicted pI of 10.6, while FAM150B has one of 9.75, and we show here that FAM150A exhibits heparin binding properties, however we have not observed a cooperative role of heparin and the FAM150 ligands in ALK activation as has been described for the fibroblast growth factor receptors and FGF.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: FAM150 ligands can bind an ALK-LTK heterodimer complex.
source: Our data also suggest that FAM150 ligands can bind an ALK-LTK heterodimer complex.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: ALK and LTK have been reported to be coexpressed in the mouse hippocampus.
source: While the physiological significance of such an interaction is currently unclear, ALK and LTK have been reported to be coexpressed in some tissues, such as the mouse hippocampus (Weiss et al., 2012), where such an interaction may be important.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2012.

claim: FAM150 proteins do not seem to be conserved outside the vertebrates.
source: FAM150 proteins do not seem to be conserved outside the vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the evolutionary distribution of FAM150 proteins.

claim: In zebrafish there are three FAM150 proteins (FAM150ba, FAM150bb and FAM150A).
source: In zebrafish there are three FAM150 proteins (FAM150ba, FAM150bb and FAM150A), while in mouse and humans only FAM150A and FAM150B exist (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: In mouse and humans only FAM150A and FAM150B exist.
source: In zebrafish there are three FAM150 proteins (FAM150ba, FAM150bb and FAM150A), while in mouse and humans only FAM150A and FAM150B exist (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: The Drosophila Jeb ligand is unable to activate either mouse or human ALK.
source: The Drosophila Jeb ligand is unable to activate either mouse or human ALK (Yang et al., 2007), and to date, no Jeb-like ligand for vertebrate ALKs has been reported.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2007.

claim: No Jeb-like ligand for vertebrate ALKs has been reported to date.
source: The Drosophila Jeb ligand is unable to activate either mouse or human ALK (Yang et al., 2007), and to date, no Jeb-like ligand for vertebrate ALKs has been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the current state of knowledge.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are not only able to activate the wild-type ALK receptor, but also to 'superactivate' mutant ALK receptors.
source: The finding that FAM150A and FAM150B are not only able to activate the wild-type receptor, but also to 'superactivate' mutant ALK receptors, is important in this context.

claim: FAM150A and FAM150B are expressed in adrenal gland and thyroid.
